extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor organizations, labor attorneys, HR professionals, and other stakeholders engaged in NLRA joint-employer determinations or rulemaking comments
extracted.subtask_description: Defines how the NLRB determines when two or more entities are joint employers under the National Labor Relations Act, including what counts as control (direct, indirect, or reserved) and which terms and conditions are ‘essential.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority or exercise of control over essential terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A common-law employer of particular employees shares or codetermines matters governing employees' essential terms and conditions of employment if the employer possesses the authority to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both) or exercises the power to control (whether directly, indirectly, or both) one or more of the employees' essential terms and conditions of employment, regardless of whether the employer exercises such control or the manner in which such control is exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule focuses on whether a putative joint employer 'possesses the authority to control or exercises the power to control' essential terms; possession of authority (even if not exercised) or indirect exercise (e.g., through intermediary) can suffice. This standard incorporates common-law agency principles and applies irrespective of the manner of exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive list of 'essential terms and conditions of employment'
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides an exhaustive list of seven categories of terms or conditions considered 'essential' for the joint-employer inquiry: (1) wages, benefits, and other compensation; (2) hours of work and scheduling; (3) the assignment of duties to be performed; (4) the supervision of the performance of duties; (5) work rules and directions governing the manner, means, and methods of the performance of duties and the grounds for discipline; (6) the tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge; and (7) working conditions related to the safety and health of employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These seven categories narrow the Board's inquiry to those elements most relevant to Section 8(a)(5) and 8(d) bargaining rights, while implementing the common-law focus on 'all of the incidents of the relationship' directed at essential terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved (unexercised) authority can suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of an unexercised contractual reservation of the right to affect essential terms or other forms of reserved authority may be sufficient to render an entity a joint employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board rejects an 'actual-exercise' requirement; case law (e.g., Global Horizons) supports that never-exercised but reserved authority over essential matters (e.g., legally obligated provision of wages/benefits) can establish joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control (including through intermediaries) can establish joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that an employer has actually exercised control over essential terms and conditions of another employer's employees, whether directly or indirectly (such as through an intermediary), can suffice to establish a joint-employer relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect control examples include recommending discipline that is implemented by the staffing employer, communicating work assignments to another entity's managers, or exercising detailed ongoing oversight of how individual tasks are performed. The common law permits consideration of attenuated forms of control and rejects use of intermediaries to avoid master-servant relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of control must be an essential term
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting that possession of unexercised authority or indirect control is sufficient, the relevant object of that control must be an essential term or condition of employment as defined by the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board clarified the proposed rule to require that, in each instance, the control (possession or exercise) be over one or more of the seven defined essential terms; possession of control over immaterial matters is not sufficient to establish joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude control immaterial to employer-employee relationship or essential terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of an employer's control over matters that are immaterial to the existence of a common-law employment relationship or that do not bear on employees' essential terms and conditions of employment is not relevant to the joint-employer inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 103.40(f) instructs the Board to disregard evidence of indirect control that the common law treats as ordinary incidents of a company-to-company or independent-contractor relationship. The Board will examine proffered evidence and determine whether it reflects ordinary contracting or indicia of an employment relationship; only the latter is probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board will not presuppose employer status from immaterial control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board does not assume an entity is an 'employer' merely because it possesses or exercises forms of control that are immaterial to the common-law employment relationship and do not bear on essential terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the distinction between ordinary company-to-company contracting and common-law agency; entities with only immaterial control will not be treated as employers under the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining obligations of joint employers
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint employer of particular employees must bargain collectively with the representative of those employees with respect to any term or condition of employment that it possesses the authority to control or exercises the power to control (regardless of whether that term is one of the seven 'essential' terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, a joint employer is not required to bargain with respect to any term or condition of employment over which it does not possess the authority to control or exercise the power to control. Thus bargaining obligations are tied to the authority/power to control, not solely to the listed essential-term categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law agency principles govern interpretation of 'employer' and 'employee'
rubrics_metrics.description: Common-law agency principles define the statutory employer-employee relationship under the Act; courts and the Board interpret 'employer' and 'employee' using the common law of agency as the primary guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board identifies sources it will consult (e.g., Restatement (Second) of Agency, judicial decisions, compendiums) and rejects the idea that the common law is too amorphous. Control is the 'touchstone' of the inquiry, and the Board follows Supreme Court and circuit precedent requiring common-law guidance (e.g., NLRB v. Town & Country Electric; BFI v. NLRB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual, case-specific inquiry — no exhaustive ex ante list of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint-employer inquiry is essentially factual and requires examining all of the incidents of a particular relationship on the record; the Board will not attempt to exhaustively define, ex ante, every factual circumstance that will evidence indirect control relevant to the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because business interactions vary greatly, small differences in how, when, and over what control is exercised will determine whether such control counts as ordinary contracting or evidence of an employment relationship. The Board expects the rule's contours to be developed through adjudication of specific factual records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application across representation and unfair-labor-practice contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint-employer definition applies in all contexts under the Act, including both representation-case and unfair-labor-practice-case contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No limitation to one context is adopted; the Board applies the standard uniformly in both types of proceedings.
